Jira is powerful for engineering teams tracking tickets and sprints, but I find it rigid and poorly adapted to modern product workflows. The pricing structure is frustrating (you pay a lot to unlock the best features). Tools like Notion offer much more flexibility for how product teams actually work. While it remains the industry standard for dev teams, I now recommend more flexible alternatives for holistic product management.

Pros

As a Head of Product with a PO/PM background, Jira excels at tracking technical work and sprint management. The integration with developer tools (Git, CI/CD) is solid. Backlog management and estimation features work well for traditional agile ceremonies. It's an industry standard, which means most tech teams are familiar with it. The reporting capabilities are comprehensive once you figure them out. For pure software development tracking, it does the job reliably.

Cons

The tool feels rigid and doesn't adapt fluidly to diverse workflows. The pricing model is frustrating, you need to pay significantly more to unlock the most valuable features, which feels like nickel-and-diming. Compared to modern tools like Notion, Jira lacks flexibility and feels stuck in an older paradigm. The ticket-centric approach is limiting for product strategy work, discovery, and cross-functional collaboration. Customization is complex and requires admin expertise. The UX hasn't evolved much and feels dated compared to newer alternatives. It's built for engineering workflows but struggles with the broader product management needs like ideation, research synthesis, and stakeholder alignment.

Alternatives considered
NotionProductboard
Reason for choosing Jira

Industry standard, many integrations, ability to build a lot of different workflows.

Switched from
Trello

Trello was not doing enough for complex workflows

Pros

What I like most about Jira is that it is a very useful and structured tool for organizing team tasks, managing requests coming from different departments, and keeping track of the progress of each activity. It helps centralize work in one place, making it easier to assign responsibilities, monitor priorities, and understand the status of each task at a glance. Jira is especially valuable for project and team collaboration because it allows different teams to work on the same workflow, share updates, leave comments, and keep everyone aligned on deadlines and responsibilities. I also appreciate its flexibility: it can be adapted to different types of projects, from simple task management to more complex workflows involving multiple teams. In terms of value for money, I think Jira offers strong value when it is used consistently by the whole team, because it reduces confusion, improves visibility, and helps manage projects more efficiently. The boards, filters, dashboards, and reporting features make it easier to follow progress and identify bottlenecks. While it is not mainly a diagram creation tool, its visual boards and integrations can still help represent workflows and project progress in a clear way.

Cons

What I like least about Jira is that, at first, it can feel quite complex and not immediately intuitive, especially when trying to find the section related to your own tasks. For new users, the platform can seem crowded with many menus, boards, filters, projects, and configuration options, so it takes some time to understand where to look and how to navigate efficiently. The learning curve is probably the main downside, particularly for people who are not used to project management tools or agile workflows. Jira becomes much easier once you understand its logic, but the initial setup and onboarding may require guidance from more experienced team members. Another aspect that could be improved is ease of use for simpler needs: because Jira is very powerful and customizable, it can sometimes feel heavier than necessary for small teams or straightforward task management. Also, when it comes to diagram creation, Jira is not the most complete solution by itself; it usually requires integrations or additional tools to create more advanced diagrams or visual documentation.

Overall, my experience with Jira has been positive. It’s a strong project management and issue-tracking platform that works especially well for agile teams managing complex workflows and collaboration across multiple projects. I found it very effective for sprint planning, backlog management, task tracking, and maintaining transparency across teams. The customization options, integrations with development tools, and reporting capabilities make it highly adaptable to different team needs. At the same time, there’s a learning curve, and the platform can feel overly complex for smaller teams or lightweight projects. Once workflows are properly configured, though, it becomes a reliable system for organizing work and improving team coordination.

Pros

What I’ve liked most about Jira is how flexible it is without losing structure. It handles everything from simple task tracking to complex agile workflows (Scrum, Kanban) in one place, and you can customize fields, workflows, and boards to match how your team actually works rather than forcing a rigid process. Another standout is visibility. Dashboards, filters, and reporting tools make it easy to see progress, blockers, and team workload at a glance, which is especially useful in collaborative or distributed teams. That said, it’s not perfect—it can feel heavy or over-engineered for smaller projects—but when used well, it becomes a powerful single source of truth for project management and development work.

Cons

What I liked least about Jira is that it can become overly complex and difficult to maintain as projects grow. The large number of configuration options, workflows, and permissions can make onboarding slower and sometimes create unnecessary process overhead for simple tasks. Performance can also feel sluggish at times, especially with heavily customized projects or large backlogs. In addition, the UI can be overwhelming for new users, and finding the right settings or filters often takes more clicks than expected.

Overall my experience with Jira has been positive. It really helps in organizing work, tracking tasks and managing sprints in a structured way. Once you get familiar with how projects and workflows are set up, it becomes easier to use in day to day work. It improved visibility across the team and made collaboration smoother. There are few usability challenges but the benefits kind of outweigh the drawbacks for project tracking.

Pros

What I liked most about Jira is how flexible it is for managing different kind of work. We used it for sprint planning, backlog tracking and day to day task updates, and it kept everything in one place which was really helpful. The boards (Scrum/Kanban) make it easy to see what everyone is working on and the progress of tickets without asking around. Also the integrations with other tools we use and the reporting dashboards are pretty useful, especially for tracking team performance and deadlines. It does take a little time to get used to, but once you start using it regularly it becomes part of the daily workflow.

Cons

One thing I liked least about Jira is that it can feel a bit heavy and complex, especially for new users. There are so many fields, workflows and configurations that sometimes it becomes confusing to just create or update a simple ticket. Also performance can be slow at times, like pages take few extra seconds to load which gets frustrating when you are working on multiple tickets. The UI also feels cluttered in some areas and could be more simplified.

I've been using Jira nearly every business day for the past 11 years. I've also used it in different implementations at 3 different companies. Each had its own unique way of incorporating the platform into its workflow. Each had its benefits, but each also has its own smaller nitpicky things that I wish Atlassion would fix. At the end of the day though, Jira is extremely powerful, and I honestly can't imagine not having it as a daily software development tool.

Pros

There's a reason is basically the gold standard for software development teams to manage their workflows. It's fully customizable, but also provides a clear path for issuing and tracking projects and development efforts. It's highly collaborative and incredibly powerful for both small and very large teams.

Cons

The platform is very slow to introduce new features. I understand not wanting to rock the boat too much, since so many people use it every single day. However, I think it's overdue for some quality-of-life UX improvements and introduction of net-new features. Also, its notification system is frustratingly so close to being good, but falls short of being useful. I'm unable to use the mobile app's push/badge notifications because there's no way of marking one as unread after opening it. Not only that, if I have 20 new updates and I open one of them, all 20 are now marked as read. Because of this, I'm forced to use email notifications to ensure I don't miss anything, but now my inbox is 70% bloated with Jira notification... Again, I just wish they would improve smaller, seemingly obvious shortcomings like this.
